2214-7829462026DecInternet interventionsInternet IntervPsychological distress over time among adolescent Soluna users: A prospective observational study.10100110100110100110.1016/j.invent.2026.101001It is critical to investigate innovative methods of providing immediate mental health support for youth. Soluna is a digital mental health and wellbeing platform for youth ages 13-25 launched and developed through a partnership between the California Department of Health Care Services and Kooth Digital Health as part of California's Children and Youth Behavioral Health Initiative. Soluna provides users with rapid access to self-help content and tools, pre-moderated peer community, coaching sessions, and care navigation from any internet-connected device.The purpose of this study is to examine mental health and wellbeing outcomes over time among a self-selected subset of Soluna users aged 14-17.We conducted a non-randomized, prospective, observational study. Participants completed three surveys (baseline, one-month, and three-months post-baseline) that assessed psychosocial outcomes and self-reported engagement with platform features. The primary outcome was psychological distress as measured by the YP-CORE. We conducted pre-registered analyses to determine whether outcomes changed among participants over the three-month evaluation period.A total of 232 participants completed baseline measures, with 136 and 98 participants retained at one- and three-month follow-ups, respectively. Participants showed statistically significant within-group reductions in the primary outcome of distress from baseline to three-months (d = 0.63), and statistically significant improvements in secondary outcomes of depression, anxiety, hopelessness, loneliness, suicidal ideation, and quality of life (r = 0.35-0.53).In this prospective observational study, participants showed statistically-significant within-person reductions in distress. Findings point towards the potential that scalable digital platforms like Soluna may offer accessible mental health and wellbeing support for youth.© 2026 The Authors. 1879-40761822026Oct16Journal of geriatric oncologyJ Geriatr OncolLoneliness trajectories and psychosocial, behavioral, and functional vulnerability among cancer survivors: A comparison of patients aged 50-64, 65-74, and ≥75 years.10465210465210.1016/j.jgo.2026.104652S1879-4068(26)01809-6Loneliness is common among older cancer survivors and may contribute to depressive symptoms, adverse health behaviors, functional decline, and loss of independence. National data on loneliness trajectories and survivorship-related vulnerability remain limited.The study cohort included cancer survivors aged ≥50 years from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, with age categorized as 50-64, 65-74, and 75 years or older. Loneliness was the primary exposure; 2020-2022 data were used to classify survivors as never lonely, or as having incident, resolved, or persistent loneliness. Survey-weighted logistic and linear regression models were used to evaluate associations between loneliness and psychosocial, behavioral, and functional measures after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics, comorbidity burden, and self-rated health, as applicable.Among 2331 cancer survivors aged 50 years or older, mean age was 72.4 years, 59.5% (n = 1387) were female, and 18.6% (n = 433) reported loneliness. In cross-sectional multivariable analyses, loneliness was associated with higher odds of elevated depressive symptom burden (aOR, 11.21; 95% CI, 7.44-16.90), loss of independence (aOR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.01-2.31), fair or poor self-rated health (aOR, 1.92; 95% CI, 1.35-2.72), and current smoking (aOR, 2.37; 95% CI, 1.06-5.29). In a separate adjusted linear regression model, loneliness was associated with a 3.10-point higher continuous Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression score (β, 3.10; 95% CI, 2.82-3.39). In longitudinal trajectory analyses, persistent loneliness (aOR, 15.78) and incident loneliness (aOR, 8.32), but not resolved loneliness, were associated with elevated depressive symptom burden.Among cancer survivors aged 50 years or older in the United States, loneliness was associated with depressive symptom burden, worse self-rated health, current smoking, and loss of independence. Persistent and newly emergent loneliness identified survivors with the greatest depressive burden, supporting repeated loneliness assessment to guide targeted psychosocial, behavioral, and functional support.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. 2227-903214192026Sep24Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)Healthcare (Basel)Dimensions of Loneliness Among Older Adults in Osijek-Baranja County: Associations with Sociodemographic, Family, and Social Characteristics.316510.3390/healthcare14193165Background/Objectives: Loneliness among older adults is a public health concern associated with adverse health and well-being outcomes, yet evidence from eastern Croatia remains limited. This study examined social loneliness, family loneliness, and loneliness in romantic relationships among adults aged ≥65 years and their associations with sociodemographic, family, and social characteristics. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 431 community-dwelling older adults in Osijek-Baranja County from January to April 2025. Loneliness was assessed using the Croatian adaptation of the Social and Emotional Loneliness Scale. Group differences and correlations were examined using nonparametric methods, followed by separate multiple linear regression models with HC3 robust standard errors. Results: Median scores were 38 (29-47) for social loneliness, 20 (14-29) for family loneliness, and 41 (27-50) for loneliness in romantic relationships. Poorer perceived family-contact quality was associated with higher social and family loneliness in the adjusted models. Compared with good-quality contact, poor-quality contact was associated with social- and family-loneliness scores that were 19.66 and 25.52 points higher, respectively (both p < 0.001). Men and suburban residents had higher social loneliness in bivariate analyses, but sex and residence were not significant in the adjusted model. After adjustment for age, never-married, divorced, and widowed participants had romantic-loneliness scores 14.66, 21.55, and 15.58 points higher than married participants, respectively (all p < 0.001). Older age was weakly and positively correlated with social loneliness (ρ = 0.148; p = 0.002) and loneliness in romantic relationships (ρ = 0.194; p < 0.001). Family-contact frequency was not significant overall in the adjusted social and family loneliness models. Conclusions: Perceived family-contact quality and marital status were associated with distinct loneliness dimensions. 1541-65772026Oct15Research and theory for nursing practiceRes Theory Nurs PractExperiences of Older Adults Living With HIV.RTNP-2026-0028.R110.1891/RTNP-2026-0028Background and Purpose: Older people living with HIV (OPLWH) face complex challenges as they age. Although advances in antiretroviral therapy have transformed human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection into a chronic condition and increased longevity, aging with HIV is often accompanied by multimorbidity, polypharmacy, stigma, social isolation, and mental health concerns. These intersecting factors complicate clinical management and are not always fully addressed in traditional HIV care models. Methods: This study aimed to explore the clinical care experiences of OPLWH over age 50. A qualitative descriptive inquiry was undertaken to gain an in-depth understanding of participants' experiences. Semistructured individual interviews were conducted with 16 OPLWH. All interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, following an iterative process of coding, categorization, and theme development to identify patterns across participants' narratives. Results: Five key themes emerged: (a) looking beyond the virus and T-cells; (b) detecting emerging health needs related to aging with HIV; (c) identifying and addressing psychological and social needs; (d) addressing barriers to accessible and coordinated care; and (e) supporting patient empowerment, advocacy, and education. Participants required more comprehensive support in advocacy, social connection, care accessibility, and care coordination. Conclusions: Findings reveal critical gaps in nursing practice and emphasize the need for patient-centered, holistic care for OPLWH. Nursing practice should incorporate comprehensive assessments that address physical, psychological, and social domains; enhance interdisciplinary collaboration; and prioritize proactive screening for age-related comorbidities, mental health concerns, and social determinants of health. 2561-326X102026Oct15JMIR formative researchJMIR Form ResFeasibility of Using a Wearable Device to Identify Loneliness Among Older Adults Living Alone: Mixed Methods Study.e94027e94027e9402710.2196/94027Addressing loneliness is a public health priority, with increasing interest in technological solutions for older adults. However, evidence on real-world feasibility and acceptability of such technologies remains limited.This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of the Conversation as Therapy (CaT) Pin, a wearable device designed to capture time spent in conversation among older adults living alone, following prototype refinement. Specifically, the study assessed whether a sufficient amount of synchronized, device-derived conversation data and self-reported loneliness data could be generated to explore the relationship between conversation time and loneliness.A 2-phase, mixed methods feasibility study was conducted. In phase 1, a Consumer Advisory Group (CAG) participated in a 1-hour discussion to inform study processes and device design, followed by a 1-week prototype test with older adults (n=3). Prototype usability, device design, and study procedures were explored through interviews and informed iterative refinement. In phase 2, community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older living alone trialed the device for 2 weeks. Participants completed activity logs capturing loneliness, activity engagement, device wear, and conversations at 6-hour intervals. Device-captured conversation time was compared with self-reported data where available. Qualitative interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to understand participant experiences of device acceptability and feasibility.In phase 1, 6 CAG participants, including 3 prototype testers, identified usability and design issues that led to modifications before phase 2. Phase 2 involved 23 participants (15 women; mean age 79.4 y, SD 6.7 y), with 7 classified as lonely using the UCLA-3 scale. However, only 8 (34.8%) participants generated sufficient concurrent device and activity log data, preventing meaningful assessment of the relationship between conversation time and loneliness. Feasibility challenges were driven by device acceptability, namely usability, comfort, aesthetics, and integration into daily life, which limited sustained wear and data synchronization. Qualitative findings indicated that participants prioritized quality rather than quantity of social interaction, and many did not perceive personal benefit from device use, citing lack of perceived need or concerns related to functionality and design. Together, methodological and conceptual challenges were identified in using conversation time as a potential indicator of loneliness.This study demonstrated that, in its current form, using a wearable device to capture time spent in conversation and align these data with self-reported loneliness was not feasible among older adults living alone. Feasibility was constrained by device acceptability related to usability, participant adherence, and data synchronization challenges. Findings also suggest that conversation time alone may be insufficient as an indicator of loneliness, given participants' emphasis on the quality and personal meaning of social interaction. These results provide practical lessons for future digital health research with older adults, including the need for early co-design, monitorable data-capture systems, and more nuanced approaches to measuring loneliness.© Rajna Ogrin, Georgina Johnstone, Bradley R Crammond, Judy A Lowthian.
